A fantastic exercise in intrigue, suspense, horror, social commentary, with well-considered player choice and interactivity. There are a great many wonderful touches to truly immerse you in using a missing person's phone. It's completely diegetic and naturalistic, never straying from the phone's interface. And if you're interested in the idea of desperately looking through someone's phone to find any trace of them, going down a deeper and deeper rabbit hole, you absolutely need to play this game. It is unmatched by any of its peers.

Just keep in mind the production value, so if you're expecting AAA industry level acting from this modest indie studio, remember this is a game made by a small team where you're on a typical phone of an ordinary woman with unremarkable colleagues. Its brilliance lies in the presentation, concept, and suspense. The production flaws and minor mechanical limitations are quick to forgive, and going through again on Begin+ easily makes up for it in my opinion.

Simulacra is a really good game, it's about the player finding a mobile phone that belonged to a person named Anna (who has been kidnapped by the Simulacra itself). When unlocking or attempting to unlock the phone, it becomes distorted (I believe it shows "HELP ME" as well, I don't remember lol). After that shows, you'll find a video that shows Anna herself, being scared and telling the player not to find her. The gameplay is honestly amazing; you can interact with her boyfriend, her friends, fix glitched messages or images, and even check apps that she downloaded. The game has specific endings depending on what you're going to go for.

It's good but you need to be able to look past 4 big faults to really get into it, as the game can kinda work on moon logic sometimes and it sets you up for failure, not to mention a few other plot holes. 

Also the story is completely railroaded, it has multiple endings but no matter which ending you're going to get, the story and game is pretty much the exact same aside from VERY MINOR character dialog and Ashley not talking to you depending on your choices, until the final scene where it will use choices you made in the past and whether or not you do a specific thing right before the final scene, to determine if Anna and Taylor, the two main characters, are destined to die, or if not, whether or not only one of them will live or if both of them are going to live.

It only branches out and stops being railroaded in the climax and resolution of the game, and since it outright encourages you to replay it to get all the endings, it can't really get away with assuming that people will only play it once, especially since it's extremely easy to fall into the worst ending if you don't do everything right.

Outside of these things, and if you can get past it, this game is good and fun, an intriguing concept and I like Taylor even if he's a total dork. But don't play the phone version as the loops in audio are not as smooth as on the PC version and I experienced a bug that ruined every FMV in the final scene, so you should get it on steam for PC like here.

I stumbled on Simulacra 2 first, I'm not really sure how, and enjoyed that immensely, so I decided to get Simulacra and Simulacra 3.

Now that I've 100% this one - Simulacra is good, but Simulacra 2 is definitely an improvement. It's been a bit since I've last played S2 *but* I recall there seeming to be a lot more variation in what happens, which I think is invaluable in a game like this. Simulacra itself, though, is still very well done. The premise is intriguing, the gameplay is intuitive, and the fact there are multiple endings is satisfying (and the non-diegetic-seeming sounds definitely fooled me a few times, as if they were truly happening). Need for more proofreading aside. it's solid and fun.
